title: 2025-04-10 Rate limits & org/project keys demo - HealthNet Systems
summary: Product walkthrough focused on rate limiting, quotas, and multi-tenant controls. Demoed org vs project API keys, per-project quotas, burst policies, and console UI for setting SLA tiers. Customer concerned about fair-share, dedicated vs hosted, and auditability. Agreed to share org-key implementation guide, pricing sheet for Reserved/Dedicated, and SOC2 summary. Follow-up POC requested for 2-week pilot scoped to their ingestion pipeline.
next_steps: Avery to send org/project keys doc, pricing for dedicated/reserved options, and SOC2 summary (by 2025-04-14)
Schedule 2-week pilot POC with HealthNet infra team (target start 2025-04-21)
Riley to run sample throughput benchmarks with HealthNet test dataset (share results)
Customer to confirm list of projects to onboard for pilot
action_items: Avery Chen - Send org/project key & quota docs and pricing - 2025-04-14
Riley Patel - Prepare benchmark plan + sample curl scripts - 2025-04-18
Maya Singh - Share pilot project list and compliance contacts - 2025-04-15
transcript:
Header: 2025-04-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42 mins | Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Riley Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (CTO, HealthNet), Liam O'Connor (Lead Platform Eng), Sofia Alvarez (Security), Benji (SRE)

[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Avery from Redwood Inference. Today's agenda — quick intro, then Riley will demo rate limits, org and project keys in the Console and API, then Q&A.

[00:12] Maya Singh: Hi, thanks. We wanted to focus this meeting on how you handle multi-tenant rate limits and what level of control we get per project and per org. We're onboarding a bunch of internal teams and need strong isolation.

[00:27] Riley Patel: Great, that's exactly what we planned to show. Quick note — I'll show the Console and then hit the API endpoints. Some of the field names in the demo might show up as "Redwood Optimiz" in the transcript, it's the Optimize panel.

[00:40] Liam O'Connor: Quick context — we run an ingestion pipeline that fans out to multiple product teams. Peak qps per project right now is about 120 requests/sec, and we need burst support up to ~600 for short jobs. SLAs vary by team.

[01:02] Benji: Also, how do you handle abusive tenants? We want fair-share and throttling, not full shutdowns causing outage propagation.

[01:14] Riley Patel: Good question. In Redwood you can configure both hard quotas (absolute caps) and soft rate-limits with backoff policies. Soft limits let you define a baseline QPS and a burst window. We also have token bucket-style rate limiters in front of the runtime.

[01:35] [Screen share starts] Riley Patel: Ok, I'm in the Console. Top right you see the org scope - HealthNet Org. Under Security -> API keys, you can issue an Org key or Project-specific key. Org keys have global scope and can be restricted to read-only or full access; project keys are tied to a project id and inherit project quota rules.

[02:05] Riley Patel: I'll create a demo project key now — note the UI warns if you try to use an org key for project-scoped usage. (murmur) You'll see an option for per-project daily quota, monthly quota, and also per-minute QPS.

[02:28] Sofia Alvarez: When you say org key, is that equivalent to a master admin key? What about key rotation and KMS integration?

[02:36] Avery Chen: Org keys are effectively admin; we recommend storing them in your secret manager and using rotation. We integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments and with Cloud KMS for hosted — so you can rotate keys and we keep an audit trail. We'll send the SOC2 and KMS integration notes.

[02:57] Riley Patel: Back to quotas — you can set policies at the project level: e.g., Project A gets 1k QPS sustained with 5k burst for 30s, Project B gets 200 QPS. You can also set weightings for fair-share when aggregate capacity is constrained. Those live under "Policy -> Rate & Quotas".

[03:20] [00:03:20] Riley Patel: I'm going to hit the API to show enforcement. Using a project key: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pk_proj_xxx" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate...

[03:30] [Ambient noise / typing]

[03:40] Riley Patel: If you exceed the per-project rate, API returns 429 with a Retry-After header, and the response includes the quota id and current usage. We also emit events to the audit log and can forward alerts to your slack via integrations.

[04:05] Liam O'Connor: Is the 429 behavior configurable? We prefer graceful degradation with queued requests instead of immediate 429s for some internal infra.

[04:15] Riley Patel: Yes — configurable. You can enable a queueing policy at the org-level for critical projects. Queue size, TTL, and backpressure thresholds are adjustable. For Hosted customers queueing is limited by latency SLOs; for Dedicated you can increase queue capacity.

[04:37] Maya Singh: Could you clarify Dedicated vs Hosted here? We might need predictable throughput for billing-sensitive tenants.

[04:45] Avery Chen: Sure: Hosted API is multi-tenant and usage-based; rate-limits are enforced per project/org. Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools and you get more control — you can bump quotas, change kernel configs, and we provide SLA-backed throughput. Private deployments let you run inside your VPC and connect KMS. Pricing differs; we'll send pricing scenarios.

[05:10] Riley Patel: Back to the Console — here's an example policy we use, called "gold-tier" with hard daily token quota, per-minute QPS, and a penalty-rate for overage. The UI also shows current usage, historical usage heatmap, and alerts.

[05:35] Riley Patel: Note: some of the labels in the UI (we heard a few calls where "KV cache" was transcribed as "KV cash"). Our logs and metric labels are consistent though: kv_cache_hit, kv_cache_miss.

[05:48] Sofia Alvarez: About audit logs — can we get immutable logs exported to our S3? Retention policy options?

[05:56] Avery Chen: Yes — for Hosted we provide a configurable retention window and can export all audit logs to customer S3 or SIEM. For Private deployments you control retention entirely. We'll include the audit export playbook in the materials.

[06:12] Riley Patel: Now I'll simulate a burst from multiple projects to show fair-share behavior. I'm going to run a small script that uses three project keys concurrently.

[06:30] [Script running, some typing noises]

[06:44] Riley Patel: You can see Project A got throttled to its share while Project C reached its burst allowance — the console annotated the events with reason codes (RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, BURST_CONSUMED).

[07:00] Liam O'Connor: How do you set prioritization? For example payment flows always win over analytics.

[07:10] Riley Patel: Prioritization is policy-driven. Each request can have a priority header or be associated with a SLA tier. The routing mesh respects priority and will preempt lower-priority tokens if capacity is limited. For transient spikes you can attach a pre-authorized override token for critical routes.

[07:32] Maya Singh: Is there any extra charge for priority routing?

[07:36] Avery Chen: For Hosted, priority routing that increases your effective throughput may incur overage charges. For Dedicated, that’s part of your reserved capacity conversation; we can dimension pools to match priority tiers. We'll share pricing examples.

[07:52] Sofia Alvarez: From a compliance perspective we need SSO for the Console and SAML + RBAC. Also separation of duties around keys.

[08:00] Avery Chen: We support SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC. You can limit who can create org keys vs who can create project keys. All key creation and rotation events are logged. RBAC groups sync from your IdP.

[08:18] Riley Patel: Quick note on telemetry: all token-level cost breakdowns are available. You can see per-route token usage, latency percentiles, and cost by project. This helps drive smart batching and quantization recommendations in Redwood Optimize.

[08:36] Liam O'Connor: Curious — can we set quotas not just by QPS but by tokens consumed? Some models are variable-length.

[08:44] Riley Patel: Yes, quotas can be token-based. You can set monthly token budgets per project and hard stop or rate-limit when a project exceeds token allocation.

[09:00] Riley Patel: I'm going to show the API behavior for org vs project key. First org key used for a project-bound request returns 403 with a warning if policy forbids org keys for that route.

[09:20] Benji: If a key is leaked, what's the fastest way to revoke?

[09:26] Avery Chen: Revoke in the Console or via API. You can also set automatic expiration on keys and require rotation. For Hosted we can also revoke at the org-level and force sessions to reauthenticate. Revocation events are recorded in exportable audit logs.

[09:48] Maya Singh: How do you handle per-customer isolation in the multi-tenant runtime? We need strict isolation between projects.

[09:56] Riley Patel: Isolation is handled at request and model-serving layer — per-project KV namespaces, per-project caching, and routing policies. For strict isolation we recommend Dedicated or Private where you get reserved pools and network-level isolation.

[10:18] Riley Patel: This shows policy keys: max_qps, burst_tokens, priority, token_budget_monthly. It's editable in Console or via Policy API.

[10:35] Maya Singh: That JSON — can we templatize it in our infra as code?

[10:40] Riley Patel: Yes, everything is available via REST/CLI. Many customers store policies in Terraform or our API calls in CICD.

[10:53] Riley Patel: Some small transcription artifacts: you might see model names like "redwood-infer-3" transcribed inconsistently in the recording. Ignore those; the UI is consistent.

[11:12] Maya Singh: On the PII handling front — our payloads can include patient-adjacent info. What's Redwood's default retention and can we disable logging of request bodies?

[11:25] Avery Chen: By default we store logs to support debugging, but for sensitive workloads you can disable request body retention; we can configure redaction filters and ensure payloads are not stored. For Private deployments you control all storage. We'll include the data-retention playbook in the follow-up.

[11:46] Liam O'Connor: How do you surface quota exhaustion to our apps — webhooks? Metrics?

[11:54] Riley Patel: Both — 429 responses include quota metadata. We push events to the audit stream and can emit Prometheus metrics via scraping in Dedicated or forward to your metrics backend. We also integrate with PagerDuty for alerts.

[12:10] Maya Singh: Ok — on the POC, we want to test the ingestion pipeline with 500-600 qps bursts and validate fair-share across 6 projects. Can you support telemetry export so we can replay the logs?

[12:24] Riley Patel: Absolutely — we'll provision a trial org with sample capacity and provide scripts. Riley will own benchmarks.

[12:32] Avery Chen: Quick recap of next steps — we'll send pricing and SOC2, bench scripts, and a pilot timeline.

[12:40] Maya Singh: Good. Who's the point for security questions?

[12:44] Avery Chen: Sofia, you can talk to our security lead — we'll put you in touch and share our compliance pack.

[12:52] [End of demo, closing]

[12:55] Avery Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the materials.

[13:00] Meeting ended.

Notes on transcript quality: Automated transcription had a few mis-hearings (Redwood Optimize -> Redwood Optimiz, KV cache -> KV cash), occasional speaker attribution issues; core technical details validated against UI screenshots shared in the console during the demo.
